name: Asteroids Deluxe

D4.note: watchdog counter; counts to 128 at 3 kHz

D3.note: reset flip-flop, preset by C22 charging

notes: Asteroids Deluxe is a relayout of Asteroids, not a new design: the clock, reset and watchdog circuits are identical part for part, with every designator shifted one position. Asteroids B5/C4/B4/B6/C6/D5/D4/E6 become Deluxe B4/C3/B3/B5/C5/D4/D3/E5. If you know one board you can navigate the other by subtracting one from the row number — but do not assume it, because the shift is what will send you to the wrong chip.
Same MPU warning as the rest of the family: 1.5 MHz operation means the part must be a 6502A, not a 6502.

Power-up sequence: C22 charging holds RESET low via D3 and clears D4; at about 1.5 VDC the preset and clear are released, D4 counts to 128 at 3 kHz and RESET goes high. A board stuck in reset points at C22, D3 or D4.
conflicts: Three cells are claimed twice by the IC parts lists and are therefore absent from the board map: B10 (B/C10 says 74LS157, B10 says 74LS374), D10 (D/E10 74LS157 against D10 74LS374) and F10 (F/H10 74LS157 against F10 74LS174). All three collisions are the same shape — a spanning designator from the 74LS157 row against a plain designator from another row — so either those LS157s do not span, or the plain designators are misread. The LS157 row also carries a C10 and an E10 of its own, which a genuine B/C10 span would already cover. One look at the component-location drawing settles it and recovers three devices.

The 74LS157 row in the Caberat printing reads 'O/E10' where the others read 'D/E10', and 'FiH10' where they read 'F/H10'. Both are rejected rather than guessed: O is not a row on this grid, and 'FiH10' does not parse as a designator at all.
